registers.role: outcomes, controls and linkage: longitudinal information on health outcomes, educational attainment, schooling outcomes and other social and socioeconomic data
linkage / sample frame: matching study members with both biological parents (99.4%)
sample frame and treatment: a Danish population-based case-control sample following 77,639 individuals born 1981-2005, supplying the genotypes and the psychiatric case/control status
treatment: neonatal dried blood spot samples from which DNA was extracted and genotyped on the Illumina PsychChip

registers.name_in_paper: Danish school leaving exams at the end of primary school
registers.role: outcomes: Danish and mathematics exam grades, turned into cohort-specific percentile ranks

linkages: genotyped iPSYCH individuals matched to the Danish population registries
study members matched with both biological parents at the birth registers (99.4%)
parents and other relatives matched, which links individual outcomes to parental socioeconomic background
siblings defined as individuals in the analytic sample with the same biological parents, used to build the sibling sub-sample and the family fixed effects
polygenic score weights taken from the external Lee et al. (2018) GWAS summary statistics, which do not include iPSYCH individuals

sample.universe: The 1,472,762 individuals born in Denmark between 1981 and 2005, from whom the iPSYCH study selected 77,639
sample.unit_of_observation: individual (one observation per genotyped study member); the within-family analysis uses individuals nested in families with two or more observed siblings
selection_rules: iPSYCH selects 77,639 individuals from the 1,472,762 Danes born 1981-2005: about one third (27,605) randomly selected from those cohorts, the remainder diagnosed with one or more psychiatric disorders
of an initial 86,189 individuals, 8,550 were excluded due to unsuccessful genotyping or quality control
restricted to study members of European descent (90.5%)
matched with both biological parents at the birth registers (99.4%)
without missing information on the family environment (82.8%)
with at least one relevant outcome (81.96%)
leaving 49,756 individuals, of whom 16,581 (33.3%) are controls and 33,175 (66.7%) psychiatric cases
educational-attainment outcomes restricted to the 28,331 individuals aged 25 or older in 2016
Danish and mathematics percentile ranks restricted to the 33,286 and 32,528 individuals born 1985-2000 with an observed exam
the within-family analysis is restricted to families with two or more observed siblings, about 5% of individuals in the sample
sample.period: births 1981-2005; registers, educational attainment and exam grades observed through 2016
sample.n_observations: 49,756 individuals in the analytic sample (28,331 with attainment at 25; 33,286 with a Danish exam score; 32,528 with a mathematics exam score; 1,487-1,838 in the within-family regressions)

construction_notes: The EA polygenic score is a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) GWAS of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe); that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH members

The score was constructed using all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; footnote 2 states that all SNPs were included during pruning and that imposing strict significance thresholds does not significantly alter the key findings

Genotyping on Illumina PsychChip; quality control filters for call rate, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and heterozygosity; each cohort phased and imputed against the 1000 Genomes Project phase 3 reference panel
The polygenic score was normalized to have mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample, so every reported coefficient is per one standard deviation of the score
The polygenic score excludes the sex chromosomes, so its distribution does not depend on gender

Danish and mathematics test scores are averages of cohort-specific percentile ranks on four Danish and four mathematics exams; cohort-specific ranks are used because different cohorts faced different combinations of exams, and because each exam is graded on a 7 point scale the average percentile is not precisely 50%
Disposable family income is the average of maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10; the resources dimension of disadvantage is the lowest quintile of that measure

Childhood disadvantage has four dimensions: both parents without any post-secondary education (18%); family in the lowest income quintile (20%); either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%); non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 22,927 (46%) experienced none, 14,882 (30%) one and 11,974 (24%) two or more; the benchmark disadvantaged group is the two-or-more group

The between-family regressions control for year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix; the family-control specifications add average log disposable family income ages 1-10, maternal and paternal years of education, maternal and paternal mental health history and family structure ages 0-10
The within-family regressions add family fixed effects and birth-order fixed effects and keep the gender control

Footnote 5: restricting to individuals with all four outcomes leaves about 13,000 individuals; the between-family results are said to replicate on that sample but the within-family sample becomes too small
Footnote 6: the between-family model was also re-estimated with only one child per family, with no significant differences in the findings (results available upon request)

claims.statement: A one standard deviation higher educational-attainment polygenic score is associated with 0.606 units of Years of Education at 25 in the Full iPSYCH analytic sample (between-family specification, Table 2, Panel A, col (1)).

definition.value: Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

timing.value: determined at conception; genotyped from neonatal dried blood spot samples

outcome.label: Years of Education at 25 (table column 'Y. Edu.' / 'Years Edu.')

definition.value: Years of education completed at age 25, taken from Danish register information on educational attainment; available for the 28,331 individuals aged 25 or older in 2016.

timing.value: at age 25

units.value: years of education at age 25, per one standard deviation increase in the EA polygenic score

magnitude.interpretation: The EA PGS explains 7-9% of the variation in educational attainment and schooling outcomes in Denmark, as measured by the change in R2 when including the polygenic score in the regression; the incremental R2 of the EA PGS in this column is 0.074.

estimand.time_horizon: educational attainment measured at age 25

population.description: Full iPSYCH analytic sample: study members of European descent, matched with both biological parents at the birth registers, without missing family-environment information and with at least one relevant outcome (49,756 individuals born 1981-2005)
population.period: births 1981-2005; registers and outcomes observed through 2016
population.selection: iPSYCH 2012 case-cohort design: 77,639 individuals were selected from the 1,472,762 Danes born 1981-2005, about one third randomly selected and the remainder diagnosed with one or more psychiatric disorders; 8,550 of an initial 86,189 were excluded for unsuccessful genotyping or quality control. The analytic sample is further restricted to European descent (90.5%), both biological parents matched at the birth registers (99.4%), no missing family-environment information (82.8%) and at least one relevant outcome (81.96%), leaving 49,756 individuals.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-individual variation in the educational-attainment polygenic score in the full iPSYCH analytic sample, conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix. The paper calls this the between-family model (Equation 1) and stresses that the polygenic score is not guaranteed to be exogenous.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix, the EA polygenic score is independent of other determinants of human capital. This is the condition required to read the between-family coefficient as a genetic effect, and the paper argues it does not hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues against it: polygenic scores are 'not guaranteed to be exogenous in most models', they 'often over-estimate genetic influences', and the within-family estimates fall by 40-50%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parental genotype and the genetic nurture it works through are an omitted common cause of the child's polygenic score and of the child's human capital; the paper concedes this confounder for the between-family model.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cited as the main concern with the between-family model (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018); quantified by the 40-50% fall in the within-family estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Population stratification is captured by the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cites Price et al. (2006) for the method, and concedes that principal components 'might not be sufficient to control for stratification' (Berg et al., 2019).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on the iPSYCH case-cohort selection and on the analytic restrictions (European descent, both biological parents matched, no missing family-environment information, at least one relevant outcome).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps and their retention rates are reported; Table 6 compares psychiatric cases with the randomly selected controls as an external-validity check, and Pirastu et al. (2020) is cited.

key_assumptions.assumption: The polygenic score measures genetic endowment with error, so the estimated effects are attenuated; the paper also notes it is 'far from clear what is being captured by the score'.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in the text, with a discussion of how GWAS sample size drives the predictive power of the score; footnote 2 reports that stricter SNP significance thresholds do not alter the key findings.

threats_discussed: polygenic scores are not guaranteed to be exogenous: genetic nurture, i.e. parental genotype acting through the child's environment (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018)
population stratification: principal components might not be sufficient (Berg et al., 2019)
differences in estimated genetic effects across groups can reflect differences in confounding bias across groups
measurement error in the polygenic score attenuates the estimated effects
the within-family design excludes individuals without a sibling in the sample (only about 5%)
sibling-peer effects or competition for resources would make within-family and between-family estimates differ even without omitted environmental effects
over-representation of psychiatric cases makes the iPSYCH sample unrepresentative of Denmark
the two-or-more-dimensions definition of the disadvantaged group is arbitrary
robustness_checks: within-family replication with family fixed effects (Table 3 Panel C; Table 4 Panel B)
adding observed family-environment controls (Table 2 and Table 3, Panel B)
disadvantage defined by the number of dimensions experienced (Table S1, Figures S1 and S2)
each dimension of disadvantage taken individually (Table S2)
within-family gender comparison in all-male and all-female sibling families (Table S3)
separate estimates for psychiatric cases and for the randomly selected control sample (Table 6)
re-estimation with only one child per family, reported as available upon request (footnote 6)
all SNPs included during pruning; stricter significance thresholds reported not to alter the key findings (footnote 2)
between-family results reported to replicate on the sample of individuals with all four outcomes (footnote 5)
unresolved_confounders: unobserved environmental influences correlated with the polygenic score (genetic nurture) in the between-family model
population stratification not fully captured by the first ten principal components
sibling interactions: sibling-peer effects or competition for resources
what the polygenic score actually captures ('it is far from clear what is being captured by the score')

(2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

timing.value: determined at conception; genotyped from neonatal dried blood spot samples

outcome.label: Danish school leaving exam percentile rank (table column 'Danish')

definition.value: Cohort-specific percentile rank in Danish school-leaving exams at the end of primary school, calculated as the average of cohort-specific percentile ranks on four Danish exams; exam grades exist from the year 2000 for individuals graduating by 2016, so the measure is available for 33,286 individuals born 1985-2000.

timing.value: at the end of primary (lower secondary) school; exams taken 2000-2016

units.value: cohort-specific percentile rank points in the Danish school leaving exam, per one standard deviation increase in the EA polygenic score

magnitude.interpretation: The paper reads the drop from Panel A as childhood environment partially mediating the association.

estimand.target_population: Full iPSYCH analytic sample: study members of European descent, matched with both biological parents at the birth registers, without missing family-environment information and with at least one relevant outcome (49,756 individuals born 1981-2005)
estimand.time_horizon: school leaving exams at the end of primary school (exams taken 2000-2016 by cohorts born 1985-2000)

population.description: Full iPSYCH analytic sample: study members of European descent, matched with both biological parents at the birth registers, without missing family-environment information and with at least one relevant outcome (49,756 individuals born 1981-2005)
population.birth_cohorts: 1985-2000 (cohorts with an observed school leaving exam)
population.period: births 1981-2005; registers and outcomes observed through 2016
population.selection: iPSYCH 2012 case-cohort design: 77,639 individuals were selected from the 1,472,762 Danes born 1981-2005, about one third randomly selected and the remainder diagnosed with one or more psychiatric disorders; 8,550 of an initial 86,189 were excluded for unsuccessful genotyping or quality control. The analytic sample is further restricted to European descent (90.5%), both biological parents matched at the birth registers (99.4%), no missing family-environment information (82.8%) and at least one relevant outcome (81.96%), leaving 49,756 individuals.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-individual variation in the educational-attainment polygenic score in the full iPSYCH analytic sample, conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order, the first ten genetic principal components AND observed measures of the childhood family environment.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix, the EA polygenic score is independent of other determinants of human capital. This is the condition required to read the between-family coefficient as a genetic effect, and the paper argues it does not hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues against it: polygenic scores are 'not guaranteed to be exogenous in most models', they 'often over-estimate genetic influences', and the within-family estimates fall by 40-50%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parental genotype and the genetic nurture it works through are an omitted common cause of the child's polygenic score and of the child's human capital; the paper concedes this confounder for the between-family model.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cited as the main concern with the between-family model (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018); quantified by the 40-50% fall in the within-family estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Population stratification is captured by the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cites Price et al. (2006) for the method, and concedes that principal components 'might not be sufficient to control for stratification' (Berg et al., 2019).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on the iPSYCH case-cohort selection and on the analytic restrictions (European descent, both biological parents matched, no missing family-environment information, at least one relevant outcome).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps and their retention rates are reported; Table 6 compares psychiatric cases with the randomly selected controls as an external-validity check, and Pirastu et al. (2020) is cited.

key_assumptions.assumption: The polygenic score measures genetic endowment with error, so the estimated effects are attenuated; the paper also notes it is 'far from clear what is being captured by the score'.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in the text, with a discussion of how GWAS sample size drives the predictive power of the score; footnote 2 reports that stricter SNP significance thresholds do not alter the key findings.

key_assumptions.assumption: The observed family-environment controls (log disposable family income ages 1-10, maternal and paternal years of education, maternal and paternal mental health history, family structure ages 0-10) stand in for the childhood environment that mediates the polygenic score's association with human capital.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reads the fall in the coefficient from Panel A to Panel B as childhood environment partially mediating the association.

Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. claims.statement: A one standard deviation higher educational-attainment polygenic score is associated with 0.072 units of Any Post Secondary Education by 25 in the Full iPSYCH analytic sample, disadvantaged group (between-family specification, Table 4, Panel A, col (4)).

definition.value: Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

timing.value: determined at conception; genotyped from neonatal dried blood spot samples

outcome.label: Any Post Secondary Education by 25 (table column 'Any P.S.E.' / 'Post Sec. Edu.')

definition.value: Indicator for having attended any post-secondary education by age 25, from Danish register information on educational attainment; available for the 28,331 individuals aged 25 or older in 2016. Table 1 reports it 'in the form of percentages divided by 100'.

timing.value: by age 25

units.value: change in the probability of any post-secondary education by age 25 (0-1 indicator units), per one standard deviation increase in the EA polygenic score; the text states the same coefficients in percentage points

estimand.target_population: Full iPSYCH analytic sample, disadvantaged group: individuals who experienced two or more of the four dimensions of childhood disadvantage (11,974 individuals, 24% of the sample)
estimand.time_horizon: attendance of a post-secondary programme by age 25

population.description: Full iPSYCH analytic sample, disadvantaged group: individuals who experienced two or more of the four dimensions of childhood disadvantage (11,974 individuals, 24% of the sample)
population.period: births 1981-2005; registers and outcomes observed through 2016
subgroups_defined: disadvantaged (two or more dimensions of childhood disadvantage)
population.selection: iPSYCH 2012 case-cohort design: 77,639 individuals were selected from the 1,472,762 Danes born 1981-2005, about one third randomly selected and the remainder diagnosed with one or more psychiatric disorders; 8,550 of an initial 86,189 were excluded for unsuccessful genotyping or quality control. The analytic sample is further restricted to European descent (90.5%), both biological parents matched at the birth registers (99.4%), no missing family-environment information (82.8%) and at least one relevant outcome (81.96%), leaving 49,756 individuals.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-individual variation in the educational-attainment polygenic score in the full iPSYCH analytic sample, conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix. The paper calls this the between-family model (Equation 1) and stresses that the polygenic score is not guaranteed to be exogenous.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix, the EA polygenic score is independent of other determinants of human capital. This is the condition required to read the between-family coefficient as a genetic effect, and the paper argues it does not hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues against it: polygenic scores are 'not guaranteed to be exogenous in most models', they 'often over-estimate genetic influences', and the within-family estimates fall by 40-50%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parental genotype and the genetic nurture it works through are an omitted common cause of the child's polygenic score and of the child's human capital; the paper concedes this confounder for the between-family model.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cited as the main concern with the between-family model (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018); quantified by the 40-50% fall in the within-family estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Population stratification is captured by the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cites Price et al. (2006) for the method, and concedes that principal components 'might not be sufficient to control for stratification' (Berg et al., 2019).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on the iPSYCH case-cohort selection and on the analytic restrictions (European descent, both biological parents matched, no missing family-environment information, at least one relevant outcome).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps and their retention rates are reported; Table 6 compares psychiatric cases with the randomly selected controls as an external-validity check, and Pirastu et al. (2020) is cited.

key_assumptions.assumption: The polygenic score measures genetic endowment with error, so the estimated effects are attenuated; the paper also notes it is 'far from clear what is being captured by the score'.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in the text, with a discussion of how GWAS sample size drives the predictive power of the score; footnote 2 reports that stricter SNP significance thresholds do not alter the key findings.

key_assumptions.assumption: Differences in the estimated genetic effect across groups reflect differences in genetic returns rather than differences in confounding bias across groups.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper raises exactly this concern for between-family group comparisons and answers it by re-running the comparison within families (Table 4 Panel B).

differences in estimated genetic effects across groups can reflect differences in confounding bias across groups
measurement error in the polygenic score attenuates the estimated effects
the within-family design excludes individuals without a sibling in the sample (only about 5%)
sibling-peer effects or competition for resources would make within-family and between-family estimates differ even without omitted environmental effects
over-representation of psychiatric cases makes the iPSYCH sample unrepresentative of Denmark
the two-or-more-dimensions definition of the disadvantaged group is arbitrary
robustness_checks: within-family replication with family fixed effects (Table 3 Panel C; Table 4 Panel B)
adding observed family-environment controls (Table 2 and Table 3, Panel B)
disadvantage defined by the number of dimensions experienced (Table S1, Figures S1 and S2)
each dimension of disadvantage taken individually (Table S2)
within-family gender comparison in all-male and all-female sibling families (Table S3)
separate estimates for psychiatric cases and for the randomly selected control sample (Table 6)
re-estimation with only one child per family, reported as available upon request (footnote 6)
all SNPs included during pruning; stricter significance thresholds reported not to alter the key findings (footnote 2)
between-family results reported to replicate on the sample of individuals with all four outcomes (footnote 5)

definition.value: Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. population.selection: iPSYCH 2012 case-cohort design: 77,639 individuals were selected from the 1,472,762 Danes born 1981-2005, about one third randomly selected and the remainder diagnosed with one or more psychiatric disorders; 8,550 of an initial 86,189 were excluded for unsuccessful genotyping or quality control. key_assumptions.supported_by: Flagged as an unresolved concern; no test or bound is offered.

definition.value: Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

timing.value: determined at conception; genotyped from neonatal dried blood spot samples

outcome.label: Any Post Secondary Education by 25 (table column 'Any P.S.E.' / 'Post Sec. Edu.')

definition.value: Indicator for having attended any post-secondary education by age 25, from Danish register information on educational attainment; available for the 28,331 individuals aged 25 or older in 2016. Table 1 reports it 'in the form of percentages divided by 100'.

timing.value: by age 25

units.value: change in the probability of any post-secondary education by age 25 (0-1 indicator units), per one standard deviation increase in the EA polygenic score; the text states the same coefficients in percentage points

estimand.target_population: Sibling sub-sample, disadvantaged group: siblings who experienced two or more of the four dimensions of childhood disadvantage
estimand.compliers: Siblings with the same biological parents who differ in their educational-attainment polygenic score: the estimate is identified from these within-family differences, and only about 5% of individuals in the sample are in families with a second observed sibling.
estimand.time_horizon: attendance of a post-secondary programme by age 25

population.description: Sibling sub-sample, disadvantaged group: siblings who experienced two or more of the four dimensions of childhood disadvantage
population.period: births 1981-2005; registers and outcomes observed through 2016
subgroups_defined: families with two or more observed siblings
disadvantaged (two or more dimensions of childhood disadvantage)
population.selection: iPSYCH 2012 case-cohort design: 77,639 individuals were selected from the 1,472,762 Danes born 1981-2005, about one third randomly selected and the remainder diagnosed with one or more psychiatric disorders; 8,550 of an initial 86,189 were excluded for unsuccessful genotyping or quality control. The analytic sample is further restricted to European descent (90.5%), both biological parents matched at the birth registers (99.4%), no missing family-environment information (82.8%) and at least one relevant outcome (81.96%), leaving 49,756 individuals.

identification.source_of_variation: Genetic variation across siblings within the same family: conditional on parental genotype, child genotype is randomly assigned at conception, so sibling differences in the polygenic score are independent of any environmental effect shared by siblings. Family fixed effects absorb all shared family influences (within-family model, Equation 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on parental genotype, child genotype is randomly assigned at conception, so genetic variation across a pair of siblings is independent of any environmental effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted with citations (Conley and Fletcher, 2017; Rietveld et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2018); no test of it is run in the paper.

key_assumptions.assumption: The family fixed effect controls for any environmental influence shared by siblings, so what remains is the impact of genetic differences.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, citing Domingue et al. (2015); the comparison of Table 3 Panel A with Panel C is the evidence offered that it changes the estimate.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interactions between siblings: the model assumes away sibling-peer effects and competition for resources, which would otherwise make within-family and between-family estimates differ even without omitted environmental effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Flagged as an unresolved concern; no test or bound is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The within-family design conditions on having a second observed sibling in the sample, which only about 5% of individuals do.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the drawback of the design; no reweighting or comparison of siblings to non-siblings is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on the iPSYCH case-cohort selection and on the analytic restrictions (European descent, both biological parents matched, no missing family-environment information, at least one relevant outcome).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps and their retention rates are reported; Table 6 compares psychiatric cases with the randomly selected controls as an external-validity check, and Pirastu et al. (2020) is cited.

key_assumptions.assumption: The polygenic score measures genetic endowment with error, so the estimated effects are attenuated; the paper also notes it is 'far from clear what is being captured by the score'.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in the text, with a discussion of how GWAS sample size drives the predictive power of the score; footnote 2 reports that stricter SNP significance thresholds do not alter the key findings.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sibling sub-sample is large enough to distinguish the group-specific effects; the paper states the reduced sample size costs it power.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated explicitly; the within-family standard errors are an order of magnitude larger than the between-family ones.

threats_discussed: polygenic scores are not guaranteed to be exogenous: genetic nurture, i.e. parental genotype acting through the child's environment (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018)
population stratification: principal components might not be sufficient (Berg et al., 2019)
differences in estimated genetic effects across groups can reflect differences in confounding bias across groups
measurement error in the polygenic score attenuates the estimated effects
the within-family design excludes individuals without a sibling in the sample (only about 5%)
sibling-peer effects or competition for resources would make within-family and between-family estimates differ even without omitted environmental effects
over-representation of psychiatric cases makes the iPSYCH sample unrepresentative of Denmark
the two-or-more-dimensions definition of the disadvantaged group is arbitrary
robustness_checks: within-family replication with family fixed effects (Table 3 Panel C; Table 4 Panel B)
adding observed family-environment controls (Table 2 and Table 3, Panel B)
disadvantage defined by the number of dimensions experienced (Table S1, Figures S1 and S2)
each dimension of disadvantage taken individually (Table S2)
within-family gender comparison in all-male and all-female sibling families (Table S3)
separate estimates for psychiatric cases and for the randomly selected control sample (Table 6)
re-estimation with only one child per family, reported as available upon request (footnote 6)
all SNPs included during pruning; stricter significance thresholds reported not to alter the key findings (footnote 2)
between-family results reported to replicate on the sample of individuals with all four outcomes (footnote 5)
unresolved_confounders: unobserved environmental influences correlated with the polygenic score (genetic nurture) in the between-family model
population stratification not fully captured by the first ten principal components
sibling interactions: sibling-peer effects or competition for resources
what the polygenic score actually captures ('it is far from clear what is being captured by the score')

ambiguities: estimand.horizon is recorded as 25 years, point_in_time, from the paper's 'at age 25' / 'by age 25' and the fact that the polygenic score is fixed at conception; the paper states no horizon relative to treatment.

definition.value: Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes. In this specification the EA PGS enters together with an interaction with the disadvantage indicator, so this coefficient is the association in the non-disadvantaged reference group.

(2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes. In this specification the EA PGS enters together with an interaction with the disadvantage indicator, so this coefficient is the association in the non-disadvantaged reference group.

timing.value: determined at conception; genotyped from neonatal dried blood spot samples

outcome.label: Danish school leaving exam percentile rank (table column 'Danish')

definition.value: Cohort-specific percentile rank in Danish school-leaving exams at the end of primary school, calculated as the average of cohort-specific percentile ranks on four Danish exams; exam grades exist from the year 2000 for individuals graduating by 2016, so the measure is available for 33,286 individuals born 1985-2000.

timing.value: at the end of primary (lower secondary) school; exams taken 2000-2016

units.value: cohort-specific percentile rank points in the Danish school leaving exam, per one standard deviation increase in the EA polygenic score

estimand.target_population: Full iPSYCH analytic sample, males only
estimand.time_horizon: school leaving exams at the end of primary school (exams taken 2000-2016 by cohorts born 1985-2000)

population.description: Full iPSYCH analytic sample, males only
population.birth_cohorts: 1985-2000 (cohorts with an observed school leaving exam)
population.period: births 1981-2005; registers and outcomes observed through 2016
subgroups_defined: males
population.selection: iPSYCH 2012 case-cohort design: 77,639 individuals were selected from the 1,472,762 Danes born 1981-2005, about one third randomly selected and the remainder diagnosed with one or more psychiatric disorders; 8,550 of an initial 86,189 were excluded for unsuccessful genotyping or quality control. The analytic sample is further restricted to European descent (90.5%), both biological parents matched at the birth registers (99.4%), no missing family-environment information (82.8%) and at least one relevant outcome (81.96%), leaving 49,756 individuals.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-individual variation in the educational-attainment polygenic score in the full iPSYCH analytic sample, conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix. The paper calls this the between-family model (Equation 1) and stresses that the polygenic score is not guaranteed to be exogenous.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix, the EA polygenic score is independent of other determinants of human capital. This is the condition required to read the between-family coefficient as a genetic effect, and the paper argues it does not hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues against it: polygenic scores are 'not guaranteed to be exogenous in most models', they 'often over-estimate genetic influences', and the within-family estimates fall by 40-50%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parental genotype and the genetic nurture it works through are an omitted common cause of the child's polygenic score and of the child's human capital; the paper concedes this confounder for the between-family model.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cited as the main concern with the between-family model (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018); quantified by the 40-50% fall in the within-family estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Population stratification is captured by the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cites Price et al. (2006) for the method, and concedes that principal components 'might not be sufficient to control for stratification' (Berg et al., 2019).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on the iPSYCH case-cohort selection and on the analytic restrictions (European descent, both biological parents matched, no missing family-environment information, at least one relevant outcome).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps and their retention rates are reported; Table 6 compares psychiatric cases with the randomly selected controls as an external-validity check, and Pirastu et al. (2020) is cited.

key_assumptions.assumption: The polygenic score measures genetic endowment with error, so the estimated effects are attenuated; the paper also notes it is 'far from clear what is being captured by the score'.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in the text, with a discussion of how GWAS sample size drives the predictive power of the score; footnote 2 reports that stricter SNP significance thresholds do not alter the key findings.

key_assumptions.assumption: Differences in the estimated genetic effect across groups reflect differences in genetic returns rather than differences in confounding bias across groups.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper raises exactly this concern for between-family group comparisons and answers it by re-running the comparison within families (Table 4 Panel B).

threats_discussed: polygenic scores are not guaranteed to be exogenous: genetic nurture, i.e. parental genotype acting through the child's environment (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018)
population stratification: principal components might not be sufficient (Berg et al., 2019)
differences in estimated genetic effects across groups can reflect differences in confounding bias across groups
measurement error in the polygenic score attenuates the estimated effects
the within-family design excludes individuals without a sibling in the sample (only about 5%)
sibling-peer effects or competition for resources would make within-family and between-family estimates differ even without omitted environmental effects
over-representation of psychiatric cases makes the iPSYCH sample unrepresentative of Denmark
the two-or-more-dimensions definition of the disadvantaged group is arbitrary
robustness_checks: within-family replication with family fixed effects (Table 3 Panel C; Table 4 Panel B)
adding observed family-environment controls (Table 2 and Table 3, Panel B)
disadvantage defined by the number of dimensions experienced (Table S1, Figures S1 and S2)
each dimension of disadvantage taken individually (Table S2)
within-family gender comparison in all-male and all-female sibling families (Table S3)
separate estimates for psychiatric cases and for the randomly selected control sample (Table 6)
re-estimation with only one child per family, reported as available upon request (footnote 6)
all SNPs included during pruning; stricter significance thresholds reported not to alter the key findings (footnote 2)
between-family results reported to replicate on the sample of individuals with all four outcomes (footnote 5)
unresolved_confounders: unobserved environmental influences correlated with the polygenic score (genetic nurture) in the between-family model
population stratification not fully captured by the first ten principal components
sibling interactions: sibling-peer effects or competition for resources
what the polygenic score actually captures ('it is far from clear what is being captured by the score')

claims.statement: The return to the educational-attainment polygenic score for Years of Education at 25 is -0.262 units different in the disadvantaged group than in the reference group (Table 5, col (1)).

treatment.label: EA PGS x Disad. (EA polygenic score interacted with childhood disadvantage)

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and the childhood-disadvantage indicator. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. The coefficient is the difference in the EA PGS slope between the disadvantaged and the non-disadvantaged group inside this specification; the non-disadvantaged group is the omitted category. Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

treatment.label: EA PGS x Disad. (EA polygenic score interacted with childhood disadvantage)

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and the childhood-disadvantage indicator. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. The coefficient is the difference in the EA PGS slope between the disadvantaged and the non-disadvantaged group inside this specification; the non-disadvantaged group is the omitted category. Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and the childhood-disadvantage indicator. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. definition.value: Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes. In this specification the EA PGS enters together with an interaction with the disadvantage indicator, so this coefficient is the association in the non-disadvantaged reference group.

definition.value: Cohort-specific percentile rank in Danish school-leaving exams at the end of primary school, calculated as the average of cohort-specific percentile ranks on four Danish exams; exam grades exist from the year 2000 for individuals graduating by 2016, so the measure is available for 33,286 individuals born 1985-2000.

timing.value: at the end of primary (lower secondary) school; exams taken 2000-2016

units.value: cohort-specific percentile rank points in the Danish school leaving exam, per one standard deviation increase in the EA polygenic score

population.selection: iPSYCH 2012 case-cohort design: 77,639 individuals were selected from the 1,472,762 Danes born 1981-2005, about one third randomly selected and the remainder diagnosed with one or more psychiatric disorders; 8,550 of an initial 86,189 were excluded for unsuccessful genotyping or quality control. The analytic sample is further restricted to European descent (90.5%), both biological parents matched at the birth registers (99.4%), no missing family-environment information (82.8%) and at least one relevant outcome (81.96%), leaving 49,756 individuals.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-individual variation in the educational-attainment polygenic score in the full iPSYCH analytic sample, conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix. The paper calls this the between-family model (Equation 1) and stresses that the polygenic score is not guaranteed to be exogenous.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix, the EA polygenic score is independent of other determinants of human capital. This is the condition required to read the between-family coefficient as a genetic effect, and the paper argues it does not hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues against it: polygenic scores are 'not guaranteed to be exogenous in most models', they 'often over-estimate genetic influences', and the within-family estimates fall by 40-50%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parental genotype and the genetic nurture it works through are an omitted common cause of the child's polygenic score and of the child's human capital; the paper concedes this confounder for the between-family model.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cited as the main concern with the between-family model (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018); quantified by the 40-50% fall in the within-family estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Population stratification is captured by the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cites Price et al. (2006) for the method, and concedes that principal components 'might not be sufficient to control for stratification' (Berg et al., 2019).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on the iPSYCH case-cohort selection and on the analytic restrictions (European descent, both biological parents matched, no missing family-environment information, at least one relevant outcome).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps and their retention rates are reported; Table 6 compares psychiatric cases with the randomly selected controls as an external-validity check, and Pirastu et al. (2020) is cited.

key_assumptions.assumption: The polygenic score measures genetic endowment with error, so the estimated effects are attenuated; the paper also notes it is 'far from clear what is being captured by the score'.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in the text, with a discussion of how GWAS sample size drives the predictive power of the score; footnote 2 reports that stricter SNP significance thresholds do not alter the key findings.

key_assumptions.assumption: Differences in the estimated genetic effect across groups reflect differences in genetic returns rather than differences in confounding bias across groups.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper raises exactly this concern for between-family group comparisons and answers it by re-running the comparison within families (Table 4 Panel B).

claims.statement: The return to the educational-attainment polygenic score for Years of Education at 25 is -0.138 units different in the disadvantaged group than in the reference group (Table 6, col (1)).

treatment.label: EA PGS x Disad. (EA polygenic score interacted with childhood disadvantage)

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and the childhood-disadvantage indicator. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. The coefficient is the difference in the EA PGS slope between the disadvantaged and the non-disadvantaged group inside this specification; the non-disadvantaged group is the omitted category. Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

claims.statement: The return to the educational-attainment polygenic score for Years of Education at 25 is -0.132 units different in the disadvantaged group than in the reference group (Table 6, col (2)).

treatment.label: EA PGS x Disad. (EA polygenic score interacted with childhood disadvantage)

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and the childhood-disadvantage indicator. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. The coefficient is the difference in the EA PGS slope between the disadvantaged and the non-disadvantaged group inside this specification; the non-disadvantaged group is the omitted category. Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

claims.statement: The return to the educational-attainment polygenic score for Mathematics school leaving exam percentile rank is -1.642 units different in the disadvantaged group than in the reference group (Table 6, col (7)).

treatment.label: EA PGS x Disad. (EA polygenic score interacted with childhood disadvantage)

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and the childhood-disadvantage indicator. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. The coefficient is the difference in the EA PGS slope between the disadvantaged and the non-disadvantaged group inside this specification; the non-disadvantaged group is the omitted category. Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

definition.value: The 'Group Differences' row of Table 6: the EA PGS x Disad. interaction estimated among iPSYCH psychiatric cases minus the same interaction estimated among the controls randomly selected from the Danish 1981-2005 birth cohorts. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions.

population.selection: iPSYCH 2012 case-cohort design: 77,639 individuals were selected from the 1,472,762 Danes born 1981-2005, about one third randomly selected and the remainder diagnosed with one or more psychiatric disorders; 8,550 of an initial 86,189 were excluded for unsuccessful genotyping or quality control. The analytic sample is further restricted to European descent (90.5%), both biological parents matched at the birth registers (99.4%), no missing family-environment information (82.8%) and at least one relevant outcome (81.96%), leaving 49,756 individuals.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-individual variation in the educational-attainment polygenic score in the full iPSYCH analytic sample, conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix. The paper calls this the between-family model (Equation 1) and stresses that the polygenic score is not guaranteed to be exogenous.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix, the EA polygenic score is independent of other determinants of human capital. This is the condition required to read the between-family coefficient as a genetic effect, and the paper argues it does not hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues against it: polygenic scores are 'not guaranteed to be exogenous in most models', they 'often over-estimate genetic influences', and the within-family estimates fall by 40-50%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parental genotype and the genetic nurture it works through are an omitted common cause of the child's polygenic score and of the child's human capital; the paper concedes this confounder for the between-family model.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cited as the main concern with the between-family model (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018); quantified by the 40-50% fall in the within-family estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Population stratification is captured by the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cites Price et al. (2006) for the method, and concedes that principal components 'might not be sufficient to control for stratification' (Berg et al., 2019).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on the iPSYCH case-cohort selection and on the analytic restrictions (European descent, both biological parents matched, no missing family-environment information, at least one relevant outcome).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps and their retention rates are reported; Table 6 compares psychiatric cases with the randomly selected controls as an external-validity check, and Pirastu et al. (2020) is cited.

key_assumptions.assumption: The polygenic score measures genetic endowment with error, so the estimated effects are attenuated; the paper also notes it is 'far from clear what is being captured by the score'.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in the text, with a discussion of how GWAS sample size drives the predictive power of the score; footnote 2 reports that stricter SNP significance thresholds do not alter the key findings.

key_assumptions.assumption: Differences in the estimated genetic effect across groups reflect differences in genetic returns rather than differences in confounding bias across groups.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper raises exactly this concern for between-family group comparisons and answers it by re-running the comparison within families (Table 4 Panel B).

claims.statement: A one standard deviation higher educational-attainment polygenic score is associated with 0.562 units of Years of Education at 25 in the Full iPSYCH analytic sample (between-family specification, Table S1, col (1)).

definition.value: Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). It excludes the sex chromosomes. In this specification the EA PGS enters together with an interaction with the disadvantage indicator, so this coefficient is the association in the non-disadvantaged reference group.

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and an indicator for experiencing 1 Disad. Meas. of childhood disadvantage, out of the four dimensions. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. The omitted category is the group with no dimension of disadvantage. Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. The omitted category is the group with no dimension of disadvantage. Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues against it: polygenic scores are 'not guaranteed to be exogenous in most models', they 'often over-estimate genetic influences', and the within-family estimates fall by 40-50%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parental genotype and the genetic nurture it works through are an omitted common cause of the child's polygenic score and of the child's human capital; the paper concedes this confounder for the between-family model.

key_assumptions.assumption: The polygenic score measures genetic endowment with error, so the estimated effects are attenuated; the paper also notes it is 'far from clear what is being captured by the score'.

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and an indicator for experiencing 3 or 4 Disad. Meas. of childhood disadvantage, out of the four dimensions. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. The omitted category is the group with no dimension of disadvantage. Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and an indicator for experiencing 3 or 4 Disad. Meas. of childhood disadvantage, out of the four dimensions. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. The omitted category is the group with no dimension of disadvantage. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.

definition.value: Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. In this specification the EA PGS enters together with an interaction with the disadvantage indicator, so this coefficient is the association in the non-disadvantaged reference group.

claims.statement: A one standard deviation higher educational-attainment polygenic score is associated with 0.124 units of Any Post Secondary Education by 25 in the Full iPSYCH analytic sample (between-family specification, Table S2, Panel D: Disadvantage = Living in a broken family ages 0-10, col (2)).

definition.value: Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes. In this specification the EA PGS enters together with an interaction with the disadvantage indicator, so this coefficient is the association in the non-disadvantaged reference group.

timing.value: determined at conception; genotyped from neonatal dried blood spot samples

definition.value: Indicator for having attended any post-secondary education by age 25, from Danish register information on educational attainment; available for the 28,331 individuals aged 25 or older in 2016. Table 1 reports it 'in the form of percentages divided by 100'.

units.value: change in the probability of any post-secondary education by age 25 (0-1 indicator units), per one standard deviation increase in the EA polygenic score; the text states the same coefficients in percentage points

population.description: Full iPSYCH analytic sample: study members of European descent, matched with both biological parents at the birth registers, without missing family-environment information and with at least one relevant outcome (49,756 individuals born 1981-2005)
population.period: births 1981-2005; registers and outcomes observed through 2016
population.selection: iPSYCH 2012 case-cohort design: 77,639 individuals were selected from the 1,472,762 Danes born 1981-2005, about one third randomly selected and the remainder diagnosed with one or more psychiatric disorders; 8,550 of an initial 86,189 were excluded for unsuccessful genotyping or quality control. The analytic sample is further restricted to European descent (90.5%), both biological parents matched at the birth registers (99.4%), no missing family-environment information (82.8%) and at least one relevant outcome (81.96%), leaving 49,756 individuals.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-individual variation in the educational-attainment polygenic score in the full iPSYCH analytic sample, conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix. The paper calls this the between-family model (Equation 1) and stresses that the polygenic score is not guaranteed to be exogenous.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix, the EA polygenic score is independent of other determinants of human capital. This is the condition required to read the between-family coefficient as a genetic effect, and the paper argues it does not hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues against it: polygenic scores are 'not guaranteed to be exogenous in most models', they 'often over-estimate genetic influences', and the within-family estimates fall by 40-50%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parental genotype and the genetic nurture it works through are an omitted common cause of the child's polygenic score and of the child's human capital; the paper concedes this confounder for the between-family model.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cited as the main concern with the between-family model (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018); quantified by the 40-50% fall in the within-family estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Population stratification is captured by the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cites Price et al. (2006) for the method, and concedes that principal components 'might not be sufficient to control for stratification' (Berg et al., 2019).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on the iPSYCH case-cohort selection and on the analytic restrictions (European descent, both biological parents matched, no missing family-environment information, at least one relevant outcome).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps and their retention rates are reported; Table 6 compares psychiatric cases with the randomly selected controls as an external-validity check, and Pirastu et al. (2020) is cited.

key_assumptions.assumption: The polygenic score measures genetic endowment with error, so the estimated effects are attenuated; the paper also notes it is 'far from clear what is being captured by the score'.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-individual variation in the educational-attainment polygenic score in the full iPSYCH analytic sample, conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix. The paper calls this the between-family model (Equation 1) and stresses that the polygenic score is not guaranteed to be exogenous.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on year-of-birth fixed effects, gender, birth order and the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix, the EA polygenic score is independent of other determinants of human capital. This is the condition required to read the between-family coefficient as a genetic effect, and the paper argues it does not hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues against it: polygenic scores are 'not guaranteed to be exogenous in most models', they 'often over-estimate genetic influences', and the within-family estimates fall by 40-50%.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parental genotype and the genetic nurture it works through are an omitted common cause of the child's polygenic score and of the child's human capital; the paper concedes this confounder for the between-family model.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cited as the main concern with the between-family model (Kong et al., 2018; Young et al., 2018); quantified by the 40-50% fall in the within-family estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Population stratification is captured by the first ten principal components of the genetic matrix.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Cites Price et al. (2006) for the method, and concedes that principal components 'might not be sufficient to control for stratification' (Berg et al., 2019).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on the iPSYCH case-cohort selection and on the analytic restrictions (European descent, both biological parents matched, no missing family-environment information, at least one relevant outcome).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection steps and their retention rates are reported; Table 6 compares psychiatric cases with the randomly selected controls as an external-validity check, and Pirastu et al. (2020) is cited.

key_assumptions.assumption: The polygenic score measures genetic endowment with error, so the estimated effects are attenuated; the paper also notes it is 'far from clear what is being captured by the score'.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in the text, with a discussion of how GWAS sample size drives the predictive power of the score; footnote 2 reports that stricter SNP significance thresholds do not alter the key findings.

key_assumptions.assumption: Differences in the estimated genetic effect across groups reflect differences in genetic returns rather than differences in confounding bias across groups.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper raises exactly this concern for between-family group comparisons and answers it by re-running the comparison within families (Table 4 Panel B).

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and the childhood-disadvantage indicator. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and the childhood-disadvantage indicator. claims.statement: The return to the educational-attainment polygenic score for Mathematics school leaving exam percentile rank is -19.68 units different in the disadvantaged group than in the reference group (Table S3, Panel C: All observed siblings are female, col math).

treatment.label: EA PGS x Disad. (EA polygenic score interacted with childhood disadvantage)

definition.value: Product of the standardized EA polygenic score and the childhood-disadvantage indicator. Childhood disadvantage: experiencing two or more of four dimensions of poor childhood environment - (i) both parents without any post-secondary education (18% of the sample), (ii) family in the lowest quintile of disposable family income, measured as average maternal and paternal disposable income at ages 1 to 10, (iii) either parent ever diagnosed with a mental health condition (22%), (iv) growing up in a broken family with non-cohabiting parents between ages 0 and 10 (28%). 11,974 individuals (24% of the sample) experienced two or more dimensions. The coefficient is the difference in the EA PGS slope between the disadvantaged and the non-disadvantaged group inside this specification; the non-disadvantaged group is the omitted category. Educational-attainment polygenic score (EA PGS): a weighted sum of single-nucleotide polymorphisms, with weights taken from the publicly available summary statistics of the Lee et al. (2018) genome-wide association study of educational attainment (all discovery cohorts except 23andMe; that study identified 1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs and did not include iPSYCH individuals). Constructed from all imputed SNPs after quality control and pruning; genotyping on Illumina PsychChip from neonatal dried blood spots, imputed against the 1000 Genomes phase 3 panel; normalized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the full sample. It excludes the sex chromosomes.
